title: Maintaining IV Patency Throughout Pharmacokinetic Studies Through a Needle-Free Blood Draw Device.
abstract: 8 8 9 Pharmacokinetic (PK) studies require temporally precise measurements of drug concentrations in biological matrices, most commonly whole blood or plasma. However, repeated venous sampling may increase participant burden and complicate PK-intensive study designs. Needle-free blood collection devices that access peripheral intravenous (IV) catheters may provide an alternative approach to repeated venipuncture while maintaining sampling schedules and specimen quality. This pilot study evaluated the feasibility of integrating the PIVO Pro needle-free blood collection device into a PK-intensive human laboratory study of inhaled Δ-tetrahydrocannabinol (Δ-THC), Δ-THC, and placebo. Participants completed a screening visit and three dosing visits conducted in a university research facility equipped with a full-scale driving simulator. During each dosing visit, venous blood samples were collected at nine time points over approximately 8 h through an indwelling peripheral IV catheter using the PIVO device. All participants reported that study procedures, including blood collection, were acceptable. Approximately 40% of vascular access sites required replacement, most commonly within the first hour and typically associated with poor initial blood return. Despite slower flow compared with standard venipuncture, sampling was generally sufficient to maintain the PK sampling schedule. One mild adverse event related to vascular access (localized bruising) was observed. These findings demonstrate the operational feasibility of needle-free blood collection through indwelling IV catheters in a PK-intensive research protocol conducted outside a traditional clinical research unit. Further studies are warranted to compare analytical performance and access durability relative to conventional venous sampling approaches.

title: SEVERE RETINAL NONPERFUSION IS ASSOCIATED WITH FEWER RETINAL LESIONS ON ULTRAWIDE-FIELD FUNDUS PHOTOGRAPHY IN PROLIFERATIVE DIABETIC RETINOPATHY.
abstract: PURPOSE: To explore the relationship between the number of retinal lesions observed on ultrawide-field fundus photography (UWF-FP) and the nonperfusion index (NPI) quantified on UWF fluorescein angiography in patients with proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR). METHODS: The NPI was measured on early-phase UWF fluorescein angiography in 100 eyes from 100 patients with PDR, including both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Eyes were divided into quartiles based on NPI values. Red dots (microaneurysms, retinal hemorrhages, and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities), venous beading, cotton-wool spots, and white thread-like arterioles were counted on UWF-FP. RESULTS: The mean NPI values for quartiles one to four were 2.8 ± 1.1%, 8.5 ± 2.1%, 17.3 ± 4.5%, and 42.8 ± 12.2%, respectively. Eyes in the highest NPI quartile (quartile 4) had significantly fewer retinal lesions on UWF-FP (76.1 ± 50.6) and fewer cotton-wool spots compared with those in the lowest NPI quartile, which showed 253.0 ± 165.5 retinal lesions ( P < 0.001). White thread-like arterioles were present in 80.0% of eyes in quartile four and none in quartile 1. Patients in quartile four were predominantly type 2 diabetics with higher rates of end-stage kidney disease, peripheral neuropathy, lower-extremity peripheral artery disease, and prior limb amputation or revascularization. CONCLUSION: In patients with poorly controlled, long-standing type 2 diabetes complicated by renal failure, peripheral neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease, or lower-limb amputation, fluorescein angiography should be considered when highly ischemic PDR is suspected, particularly in the presence of white thread-like arterioles, as it may otherwise appear milder on color fundus photography.

Eyes were divided into quartiles based on NPI values.

title: Circulating Natural Killer Cells in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes and Peripheral Neuropathy Are Altered in Their Frequency and Exhibit Impaired Functions and Angiogenic Activities.
abstract: Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and critical limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI), a severe vascular complication associated with amputation and high mortality, exhibit chronic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction. We previously reported an increased frequency of natural killer (NK) cells in advanced CLTI; however, whether NK cell alterations are already present in patients with peripheral neuropathy, which often precedes diabetic foot lesions with or without distal macroangiopathy, remains unclear. We conducted an observational pilot study to assess circulating NK cell frequency by flow cytometry and inflammatory plasma cytokines profiling by ELISA in 177 subjects stratified into five groups: healthy controls (HC, n = 25); T2DM without neurovascular complications (D, n = 26); non-macrovascular neuropathic T2DM without foot lesions (N, n = 40); non-macrovascular neuropathic T2DM with lower-limb ulcers/lesions/osteomyelitis (N1, n = 42); and macrovascular revascularized neuropathic T2DM with ulcers/lesions/osteomyelitis (NV, n = 44). NK cell subset frequencies were evaluated in an independent cohort of patients with non-macrovascular neuropathic T2DM (n = 22) and healthy controls (n = 23). NKs were further characterized for degranulation capacity, secretome composition, and pro-angiogenic activity in vitro and in vivo (Hirudo verbana). NK cell frequency was significantly increased in patients with non-macrovascular neuropathic T2DM compared with controls and was accompanied by elevated plasma levels of soluble mediators associated with NK cell activation and function, including TNF-α, IL-12p70, MCP-1, and IL-4. NKs from these patients exhibited impaired degranulation and reduced angiogenic capacity in vitro and in vivo. Their secretome is characterized by decreased release of pro-angiogenic factors and increased secretion of mediators involved in monocyte/macrophage recruitment, resulting in enhanced macrophage recruitment in vivo. If confirmed in larger cohorts, higher frequency and functional impairment of circulating NKs may act as novel therapeutic targets and prognostic biomarkers in peripheral vascular complications of T2DM.

title: Performance of Western HA-VTE risk models in East Asian populations: a prospective multicenter study.
abstract: Hospital-associated venous thromboembolism (HA-VTE) causes significant morbidity, but risk prediction models are inconsistently validated, especially in non-Western populations. We prospectively validated 5 HA-VTE risk scores (Caprini, Padua, IMPROVE [International Medical Prevention Registry on Venous Thromboembolism], Kucher, and Intermountain) in a prospective multicenter cohort of 2948 adult inpatients from 17 Chinese hospitals. Symptomatic VTE events were recorded through 3 months of follow-up. The 90-day HA-VTE incidence was 2.54%. All 5 models showed moderate discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC], 0.726-0.759). Caprini, Padua, and Intermountain models did not differ significantly (DeLong test, P> .05). Caprini had the highest sensitivity (0.83) but classified 42.6% of patients as being at high risk. Padua and Intermountain favored specificity (0.75-0.81) with lower sensitivity (0.64-0.67). Clinical model selection should align with specific balances between sensitivity and utility. In surgical inpatients, Caprini performed best (AUC, 0.804; sensitivity, 0.90; negative predictive value, 1.00), although its more than 40 input variables limit practical use. Calibration was generally acceptable. Performance varied across subgroups. The prophylaxis subgroup showed attenuated performance, with reduced discrimination (eg, Caprini AUC decreased to 0.682) and less stable calibration. Western HA-VTE models have moderate predictive value in East Asian inpatient populations. Performance differs across subgroups. Local recalibration and development of simpler, population-specific scores are needed.

We prospectively validated 5 HA-VTE risk scores (Caprini, Padua, IMPROVE [International Medical Prevention Registry on Venous Thromboembolism], Kucher, and Intermountain) in a prospective multicenter cohort of 2948 adult inpatients from 17 Chinese hospitals. Symptomatic VTE events were recorded through 3 months of follow-up.

title: Continuity of Chronic Wound Care Across Hospital-to-Home Transitions: A Qualitative Study of Hospital and Community Nurses' Experiences.
abstract: AimTo explore how hospital nurses (HNs) and community nurses (CNs) in France manage chronic wound care for older adults across settings, and how their practices shape continuity of care during hospital-to-home transitions.DesignQualitative descriptive study combining ethnographic shadowing and a focus group.MethodsFieldwork took place in a French university hospital, across four units: acute geriatrics, rehabilitation, vascular surgery, dermatology. The focus group involved CNs from seven different self-employed nursing practices. We shadowed 15 HNs for approximately 92 h and conducted one focus group with 7 CNs. Data were analyzed inductively using constant comparison, with a second-stage interpretive analysis informed by Meleis' transitions theory.ResultsFour interconnected processes shaped continuity of chronic wound care across the transition: (1) nursing expertise in wound management was expressed differently across hospital and community settings; (2) discharge coordination was fragmented, with rare nurse-to-nurse communication and insufficient transfer of wound-specific information; (3) organizational logics diverged, with discontinuous hospital workflows and time-pressured, fee-for-service-constrained community visits; and (4) patient involvement during hospitalization was limited, constraining engagement and preparedness post-discharge. Continuity was frequently maintained through compensatory work from nurses.ConclusionContinuity of chronic wound care depends less on nursing expertise than on the organizational conditions enabling that expertise to be mobilized across settings.ImpactThis study highlights the need for more integrated transitional care, including clearer and more consistent responsibilities at discharge, structured nurse-to-nurse discharge communication, and earlier patient involvement in wound care management.

The focus group involved CNs from seven different self-employed nursing practices. We shadowed 15 HNs for approximately 92 h and conducted one focus group with 7 CNs.

title: Prostatic Artery Embolization in a Patient With Bilateral Internal Iliac Artery Occlusions.
abstract: Background: Study Sample: Results: Conclusions: Prostatic artery embolization (PAE) is an established treatment for lower urinary tract symptoms due to benign prostatic hyperplasia but can be challenging in complex anatomy.An 86-year-old male with history of abdominal aortic aneurysm repair and aortobifemoral bypass presented with gross hematuria and urinary retention. Imaging and clinical evaluation confirmed BPH-related clot retention as the etiology. Careful review of preprocedural CT angiography revealed occluded bilateral internal iliac arteries, a right aberrant obturator artery (AOA) (corona mortis variant), arising from the inferior epigastric artery, which itself originated from the native right external iliac artery. The AOA supplied the entire prostate, perfusing both lobes and contributing to the contralateral pelvic circulation as well. Cone-beam CT and angiography confirmed the perfusion to both prostatic lobes. PAE was performed by accessing the native common femoral artery and selectively catheterizing the AOA. Embolization of the prostatic parenchyma was completed successfully while preserving flow to adjacent pelvic structures, avoiding non-target embolization.The patient had complete resolution of hematuria and urinary retention and remained catheter-free at 1-year follow-up.This case highlights the importance of pre-procedural evaluation and planning, demonstrating that PAE can be safely and effectively performed even in variant vascular anatomy.

title: Use of a central venous catheter as vascular access at the start of a regular hemodialysis program: impact on mortality over 2 years.
abstract: BACKGROUND: The recommended access for starting chronic hemodialysis (HD) is an arteriovenous fistula (AVF), but a (CVC) continues to be frequently used. Worldwide, its use has been associated with higher mortality, but data from Brazil are lacking. METHODS: Analytical, observational, and retrospective cohort study that aimed at analyzing the data available in the Brazilian Monthly Dialysis Registry database from Jan/2011 to Dec/2023. Using data from this registry, we evaluated the frequency of CVC use (regardless of whether tunneled or non-tunneled) at the start of HD across 13 years and assessed its impact on all-cause mortality over 2 years. RESULTS: We studied 10,182 patients. The mean age was 59 (47-69) years; 59% were male, and 33% had diabetes. CVC use at HD entry increased substantially in the last 10 years. The 2-year mortality rates for CVC and primary AVF/graft users were 20% and 9%, respectively, P < 0.001. In the fully adjusted multivariate model, the use of CVC persisted significantly associated with mortality (HR 1.69, 95%CI 1.23-2.25, P=0.001). Other variables directly associated with mortality were age (HR 1.04, 95%CI 1.03-1.05, P=0.001), and serum ferritin (HR 1.18, 95%CI 1.06-1.30, P=0.002). Serum albumin (HR 0.86, 95%CI 0.84-0.88, P<0.001) and URR (HR 0.97, 95%CI 0.96-0.97, P<0.001) emerged as protective factors. CONCLUSIONS: CVC use was associated with a 1.69-fold increased risk of 2-year mortality. The increasing use of CVCs in Brazil is concerning and highlights the need for public health strategies promoting timely permanent vascular access before HD initiation.

title: Ultrasound-guided cyanoacrylate embolization of refluxing tributaries during truncal cyanoacrylate closure (SLICE): Technique description and a proof-of-concept feasibility study.
abstract: p ObjectivesTruncal cyanoacrylate closure (CAC) does not treat refluxing tributary varicosities. We describe Side-branch Local Injection of Cyanoacrylate Embolization (SLICE) - ultrasound-guided injection of the VenaSeal adhesive into refluxing tributaries during truncal CAC - and assess its technical feasibility and periprocedural safety.MethodsSingle-center retrospective review of 32 consecutive patients (49 limbs, 58 truncal veins) treated by truncal CAC between September 2024 and December 2025; SLICE was performed in 14. The primary endpoint was technical success, defined as the absence of reflux within an injected tributary on the first postoperative duplex study. Secondary endpoints included 3-month durability, truncal occlusion, and adverse events.Results22 refluxing tributaries were injected; all were epifascial, at a median depth of 4.0 mm (range 1.2-9.6). A median of four dispenser trigger pulls was used per site (range 3-8); the series was underpowered to relate pull count to diameter (Spearman rho -0.16,= 0.50). Technical success was 21/22 (95%; 95% confidence interval 77.2-99.9) initially and 19/20 (95%; 75.1-99.9) at 3 months. On 3-month computed tomography (CT), 14 of 17 evaluable injected tributaries were occluded whereas 16 of 17 were free of reflux: anatomical occlusion lagged behind hemodynamic success. Truncal occlusion was preserved (30/30 at 1 week; 26/27 at 3 months). There was no phlebitis, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, or adhesive removal. Hyperpigmentation occurred in 3/14 patients, all with an injection <2 mm below the skin; two mild delayed hypersensitivity reactions occurred, both over the truncal rather than an injected site. One patient (7%) required re-intervention.ConclusionsSLICE is technically feasible and reproducible within a narrow range of adhesive delivery, with no adhesive-related complication at an injected site in this small series with short follow-up. Prospective comparative evaluation with patient-centered endpoints is required before efficacy can be claimed.

title: Electrosurgical septotomy across the full spectrum of aortic dissection.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Transcatheter electrosurgical septotomy divides the dissection membrane to reconstitute a single aortic lumen. Reported experience is largely confined to chronic post-dissection aneurysms. We assessed the technique across the full spectrum of descending aortic dissection, including stand-alone treatment of malperfusion. METHODS: Retrospective intention-to-treat analysis of 21 consecutive patients scheduled for septotomy between June 2022 and May 2026. The membrane was crossed by needle re-entry and divided with an electrified through-and-through guidewire at 40-60 W under fluoroscopy, without routine intravascular ultrasound or image fusion. A perfused-lumen index (perfused lumen divided by total aortic diameter) was measured before and after the procedure. RESULTS: Septotomy was performed in 20 of 21 patients (technical success 95% on an intention-to-treat basis). Indications were landing-zone preparation (57%), malperfusion (33%), preparation for open repair and true-lumen collapse. Malperfusion resolved in all 7 patients treated for that indication, and the perfused-lumen index rose from a median of 0.16 to 0.98 (18 patients, P < 0.001). There was no stroke, spinal cord ischaemia or retrograde type A dissection. Thirty-day, in-hospital and overall mortality were 10%, 14% and 19%, with one fatal delayed aortic rupture and no intraprocedural death. Three unplanned reinterventions occurred; median follow-up was 5.1 months. CONCLUSIONS: Electrosurgical septotomy was feasible across the full spectrum of aortic dissection and, in selected patients, as stand-alone treatment for malperfusion, using standard electrosurgical equipment. Given the small heterogeneous cohort and short follow-up, these findings demonstrate feasibility rather than durability.

Reported experience is largely confined to chronic post-dissection aneurysms. We assessed the technique across the full spectrum of descending aortic dissection, including stand-alone treatment of malperfusion.

title: Aspiration Thrombectomy for High-Risk Pulmonary Embolism With Life-Threatening Anemia and Active Uterine Bleeding: A Case Report.
abstract: BACKGROUND High-risk pulmonary embolism (PE) carries significant mortality, and management becomes complex when it coexists with severe anemia and active bleeding, as thrombolysis is then contraindicated. We report the case of a patient with high-risk PE complicated by severe anemia (hemoglobin 41 g/L) and active uterine bleeding from adenomyosis. CASE REPORT A 48-year-old woman presented with haemodynamic instability (blood pressure 74/47 mm Hg), critical anemia (hemoglobin 41 g/L), and a 3-year history of irregular vaginal bleeding from adenomyosis. Computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiography confirmed bilateral PE with right pulmonary artery main-trunk occlusion; echocardiography showed severe pulmonary hypertension, and duplex ultrasound showed extensive left lower-limb deep vein thrombosis. Thrombolysis was contraindicated. Emergency percutaneous aspiration thrombectomy was performed using large-bore catheters (22F, 20F, 16F) with concurrent inferior vena cava filter placement, reducing pulmonary artery pressure from 51/23 to 34/12 mm Hg; the estimated blood loss, quantified from filtered aspirate, was approximately 100 mL. Adjuncts included transfusion of 13 units of packed red cells, dilatation and curettage, gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist therapy, and titrated anticoagulation. At discharge after a 24-day hospitalization she was hemodynamically stable, and free of dyspnea, with resolved edema and hemoglobin 72 g/L, on oral rivaroxaban. CONCLUSIONS In this thrombolysis-contraindicated patient, aspiration thrombectomy with inferior vena cava filter placement was a feasible rescue strategy that achieved rapid hemodynamic and angiographic improvement without thrombolysis, with palliative rather than curative intent. As a single case, it cannot establish comparative safety or efficacy, and broader conclusions regarding efficacy cannot be drawn. It illustrates a potentially useful approach in similarly complex scenarios where coordinated multidisciplinary care is essential.

title: Adiposity and the risk of aortic dissection incidence and mortality: results from the UK Biobank, the J-SHC study and a meta-analysis of cohort studies.
abstract: trend trend trend trend trend trend trend trend trend trend 2 2 2 2 Few studies have investigated the association between adiposity and risk of aortic dissection and data is lacking on adiposity measures other than body mass index (BMI). We analyzed the association between adiposity and risk of aortic dissection in the UK Biobank, and the Japan Specific Health Checkups (J-SHC) Study, and conducted a meta-analysis of cohort studies to clarify the associations between adiposity and risk of aortic dissection. The analytical cohorts included 496,255 participants in the UK Biobank and 630,841 participants in the J-SHC Study. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to analyze associations between adiposity and risk of aortic dissection. PubMed and Embase were searched for relevant studies up to February 27, 2026. Random effects models were used to calculate summary relative risks (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the association between adiposity and risk of aortic dissection. In the UK Biobank and J-SHC, there were 371 and 105 aortic dissections during 12.3 and 4 years follow-up, respectively. In the UK Biobank, positive associations (HRs, 95% CIs) were observed between high BMI (1.54, 1.01-2.37, p=0.01), waist circumference (1.82, 1.27-2.60, p=0.001), hip circumference (1.77, 1.25-2.50, p<0.001), waist-to-height ratio (1.88, 1.30-2.70, p=0.10), and fat mass (1.36, 0.97-1.91, p=0.02) and aortic dissection risk, but no clear association was observed for waist-to-hip ratio (1.28, 0.90-1.81, p=0.08) and body fat percentage (1.09, 0.77-1.54, p=0.53). In the J-SHC Study, higher BMI (2.36, 0.98-4.84, p=0.018), waist circumference (2.26, 1.18-4.60, p=0.003), and waist-to-height ratio (2.61, 1.27-5.92, p=0.009) were positively associated with aortic dissection mortality. Five cohort studies were included in the meta-analysis on BMI and aortic dissection (2007 cases and 4,962,288 participants). The summary RR per 5 kg/mincrement in BMI was 1.09 (1.00-1.20, I = 43%), per 10 cm increment in waist circumference was 1.21 (1.05-1.40, I = 50%, n = 2), and per 0.1 unit increment in waist-to-height ratio was 1.32 (1.08-1.61, I = 39%, n = 2). These findings provide evidence for a positive association between both general and abdominal adiposity and the risk of aortic dissection, with the strongest associations observed for high waist-to-height ratio. Although further large-scale studies are warranted for confirmation, these findings suggest avoiding excess weight may be an important strategy for the prevention of aortic dissection.

title: Beyond stroke: atrial fibrillation and the broader burden of thromboembolic events in the population-based EpiHealth study.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To investigate the distribution and risk of thromboembolic events (TEs) among adults with and without atrial fibrillation (AF), and to assess oral anticoagulant (OAC) use over time. DESIGN: This population-based longitudinal cohort study included EpiHealth participants recruited between April 2011 and December 2016 and followed through linkage to Swedish health data registers from baseline until the first TE, death, or December 31, 2016. RESULTS: p At baseline, 873 of 22,616 participants (3.9%) had AF and 297 developed incident AF during follow-up. 484 participants experienced at least one TE during 70,587 person-years. Participants with AF had higher TE incidence (68 events, 5.9%; < 0.001), predominantly arterial (73.5%), with 94% of arterial events involving the cerebral circulation. Approximately one quarter of TEs among participants with AF occurred outside the cerebral circulation and comprised both venous and non-cerebral arterial events. Although participants with incident AF represented less than one quarter of participants with AF, they accounted for 40% of TEs in the AF group. OAC use increased from 39.0% to 50.4%, with a shift from predominantly warfarin to direct oral anticoagulants. In time-dependent Cox regression adjusted for age, sex, and prior arterial thromboembolism, untreated AF was associated with increased thromboembolic risk compared with no AF (HR 2.53), whereas OAC use was associated with lower risk. CONCLUSIONS: AF was associated with substantially increased thromboembolic risk, predominantly arterial in nature. One in five TEs among participants with AF coincided with newly diagnosed AF, suggesting potential opportunities for earlier AF detection and timely initiation of anticoagulant treatment.

title: Long-term outcome of stenting for the iliac vein stenosis with ipsilateral arterio-venous graft; a case series.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To analyze the possible etiology and evaluate the technical and clinical outcomes of using bare metal stents for the treatment of central venous stenosis (CVS) in the lower extremity with ipsilateral hemodialysis access. METHODS: A single-center retrospective analysis of a small case series was conducted in hemodialysis patients with lower extremity arteriovenous grafts (AVG) who were treated with bare metal stents (BMS) for symptomatic iliac vein stenosis between April 2016 and June 2021. Patients' demographic data, technical details, adverse events, clinical outcomes, and imaging data were recorded. RESULTS: The study cohort comprised seven females and four males, with a mean age of 58.8 ± 13.4 years. Preoperative lower limb venography was performed in nine patients scheduled for AVG creation. With the exception of one case demonstrating left iliac vein compression, the iliac veins were patent in all other patients. Symptoms of lower limb swelling developed at a mean interval of 9.40 ± 5.83 months (range: 3-20 months) following AVG placement. Eight cases had a concomitant history of temporary ipsilateral femoral vein catheterization. Lesion characteristics included nine stenotic lesions and two occlusive lesions. All patients were treated with SMART Control stents (Cordis Corp, USA). The technical success rate was 100%, and symptomatic relief was achieved in all cases. Over a mean follow-up period of 47.8 ± 31.7 months (range: 10-123 months), the target lesion primary patency was 100% (one-side confidence interval [CI] = 0.74,1). CONCLUSIONS: Using BMS is a safe and effective method to treat iliac vein stenosis with ipsilateral AVG.

title: Bilateral peripheral CT venography for evaluating central venous lesions in dysfunctional arteriovenous fistulas: feasibility, safety, and radiation dose in hemodialysis patients.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Central venous stenosis and occlusion are major causes of arteriovenous fistula (AVF) dysfunction in hemodialysis patients. This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility, safety, radiation exposure, and anatomical findings of bilateral peripheral CT venography for central venous assessment in patients with dysfunctional AVFs. METHODS: This single-center retrospective cohort study included 46 consecutive hemodialysis patients with dysfunctional AVFs who underwent bilateral peripheral CT venography between August 2023 and June 2025. Technical success, procedure-related adverse events, radiation dose parameters, central venous lesion characteristics, and agreement with available comparative imaging modalities were analyzed. Comparative imaging findings from puncture-based angiography and/or duplex ultrasonography were assessed descriptively. RESULTS: All 46 examinations were technically successful (100%), with a mean procedure duration of 4 minutes (range, 3-5 minutes). Minor adverse events included one patient of contrast extravasation (2.2%) and 3 of mild allergic reactions (6.5%); no severe procedure-related complications were documented. The mean CTDIvol and DLP were 11.87 mGy and 784.15 mGy·cm, respectively. Central venous abnormalities were identified in 44 patients (95.7%), including stenosis in 31 (67.4%), occlusion in 11 (23.9%), and aneurysmal changes in 2 (4.3%). Comparative imaging was available in 38 patients, and CT venography showed agreement with available findings in 37 cases (97.4%). This agreement was interpreted as descriptive concordance rather than formal diagnostic accuracy. CONCLUSIONS: Bilateral peripheral CT venography demonstrated high technical feasibility, acceptable safety, and effective visualization of central venous abnormalities in hemodialysis patients with dysfunctional AVFs. Further prospective studies are needed to validate its diagnostic performance and clinical impact. ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: This technique enables efficient, noninvasive assessment of central venous pathology with minimal risk, supporting its potential as a practical alternative to conventional imaging in hemodialysis patients.

title: Microsurgical Ligation of Spinal Dural Arteriovenous Fistula.
abstract: Spinal dural arteriovenous fistulas are a reversible cause of progressive thoracic myelopathy, for which definitive treatment requires complete disconnection of the pathological arteriovenous shunt. We demonstrate microsurgical clip occlusion and disconnection of a right T4 spinal dural arteriovenous fistula using indocyanine green (ICG) videoangiography and intraoperative neuromonitoring. Following T4-T5 laminectomy, the fistulous point was identified near the right T4 nerve root exit zone, with ICG confirming arterialized venous drainage. A clip was placed immediately adjacent to the dural fistulous point, and repeat ICG demonstrated obliteration of the shunt. The draining vein was subsequently coagulated and divided, with stable somatosensory and motor evoked potentials throughout the procedure. Precise angiographic localization and disconnection as close as possible to the dural fistulous point are critical to minimize residual shunting, vascular recruitment, and recurrence. ICG videoangiography and neuromonitoring provide valuable intraoperative confirmation for safe and definitive microsurgical treatment.

title: Microsurgical Clipping of a Posterior Communicating Artery-Incorporated Internal Carotid-Posterior Communicating Artery Aneurysm using Patient-Specific Three-Dimensional Aneurysm Models.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND INTRODUCTION: Posterior communicating artery (PCoA)-incorporated aneurysms, in which the PCoA originates from the dome, have a higher recurrence rate after endovascular treatment. Clipping is effective but technically demanding as the PCoA origin is frequently obscured by the internal carotid artery (ICA). OBJECTIVE: We present a video demonstrating microsurgical clipping of a posteriorly projecting PCoA-incorporated aneurysm using a patient-specific 3D-printed model. SURGICAL TECHNIQUE: Preoperative simulation predicted ICA obstruction of the PCoA origin. The aneurysm was dissected through the retrocarotid and opticocarotid spaces, and clips were sequentially applied, preserving the PCoA and its perforators. Indocyanine green videoangiography confirmed complete obliteration with PCoA patency. RESULT: The postoperative course was uneventful, and angiography confirmed successful clipping. CONCLUSION: Microsurgical clipping is a promising, safe, and effective alternative for PCoA-incorporated aneurysms. PEARLS AND PITFALLS: Preoperative simulation with a patient-specific 3D-printed model enables precise understanding of neurovascular relationships, contributing to safer microsurgical clipping.

title: Anticoagulation Monitoring in Recurrent Venous Thromboembolism Associated With Antiphospholipid Antibodies and Subsequent Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia.
abstract: A woman in her 20s with class III obesity and strongly positive antiphospholipid antibodies developed phlegmasia cerulea dolens and a new pulmonary embolus after recent catheter-directed thrombolysis. Before the first documented heparin administration, activated partial thromboplastin time was 95.5 s and international normalized ratio was 1.5. Eight subsequent paired samples showed activated partial thromboplastin times of 176 s to over 200 s with heparin anti-Xa activity of 0.20-0.66 IU/mL. Lupus anticoagulant testing was uninterpretable during anticoagulation, and international normalized ratio reliability was not independently established. Later thrombocytopenia prompted repeat heparin-induced thrombocytopenia testing despite an earlier negative result; a strongly positive immunoassay supported the treating team's diagnosis and transition to fondaparinux. This case illustrates the importance of selecting appropriate anticoagulation monitoring from the outset and reassessing heparin-induced thrombocytopenia when the clinical picture changes. Whether assay interference contributed to recurrent thrombosis remains unresolved.

title: Venous Thromboembolism in Patients Hospitalized With Localized, Regional, and Metastatic Head and Neck Cancer.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is a known complication in cancer patients, but data in head and neck cancer (HNC)-particularly distinguishing localized, regional, and metastatic disease-are limited. METHODS: Using the 2016-2020 National Inpatient Sample, we examined adults ≥ 18 years with HNC, excluding patients with another primary malignancy. Metastatic status was categorized as localized, regional, and metastatic. Outcomes included odds of VTE, pulmonary embolism (PE), deep vein thrombosis (DVT), inhospital mortality, and prolonged length of stay (LOS ≥ 7 days). Multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with these outcomes. RESULTS: Among 62 032 unweighted (310 160 weighted) admissions, 75.0% had localized HNC, 12.7% had regional HNC, and 12.3% had metastatic HNC; 2.6% had VTE (2.4% localized HNC, 2.3% regional HNC, and 4.1% metastatic HNC). Compared with localized HNC, regional HNC was not associated with increased odds of VTE, PE, or DVT, whereas metastatic HNC was associated with higher adjusted odds of VTE (aOR 1.52; 95% CI: 1.30-1.78), PE (aOR 1.61; 95% CI: 1.32-1.98), and DVT (aOR 1.47; 95% CI: 1.18-1.83). VTE was associated with increased inhospital mortality (aOR 1.98; 95% CI: 1.64-2.40) and prolonged LOS (aOR 2.14; 95% CI: 1.92-2.39). CONCLUSION: In hospitalized patients, distant, but not regional, metastatic HNC is associated with higher odds of VTE, and VTE is associated with adverse in-hospital outcomes including increased mortality and prolonged LOS.

title: Stenosis of a novel frozen elephant trunk in a patient with chronic dissection.
abstract: A partial elephant trunk (PET), a new type of frozen elephant trunk, was designed to prevent distal stent graft-induced new entry using a thinner nitinol wire with less radial force. We report a case of PET stenosis in chronic dissection. Total arch replacement was performed using a PET. After weaning from cardiopulmonary bypass, the lower-limb blood pressure decreased to 90% of the upper-limb blood pressure. Intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography revealed incomplete PET expansion, and on postoperative day 1, the lower-to-upper body blood pressure ratio further decreased to 70% due to PET stenosis at the steeply angulated arch. Emergency thoracic endovascular aortic repair was successfully performed, completely resolving the pressure gradient.

title: Intravascular Lithotripsy of Aortic and Renal Lesions as a Therapeutic Tool for Pickering Syndrome: A Case Report.
abstract: We report the case of a 73-year-old woman admitted with Pickering syndrome, a life-threatening condition characterized by recurrent flash pulmonary edema secondary to severe renovascular disease. Computed tomography angiography demonstrated an atrophic left kidney, a heavily calcified visceral aorta with a coral-reef morphology, and a near-occlusive stenosis of the right renal artery. Urgent endovascular treatment was performed with intravascular lithotripsy for plaque modification of the suprarenal aorta and the right renal artery, followed by renal artery stenting. The patient showed prompt clinical recovery, with resolution of pulmonary edema, stabilization of blood pressure, and improvement of renal function. This case illustrates the potential role of intravascular lithotripsy as a minimally invasive adjunct for managing severely calcified aorto-renal disease in high-risk patients, enabling endovascular treatment in otherwise challenging anatomy.

title: Transarterial Computed Tomographic Angiography in Patients With Impaired Renal Function Undergoing Endovascular Aortic Repair.
abstract: P PurposeComputed tomography angiography (CTA) is crucial for preoperative planning and postoperative surveillance of endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR). Renal function impairment however limits pre- and postoperative assessment. The aim of our study was to evaluate the safety and diagnostic value of a novel technique in the setting of patients undergoing EVAR.Methods216 patients with chronic kidney disease undergoing transbrachial placement of an angiography catheter in the aorta for contrast medium administration were analyzed retrospectively. 45 patients with normal kidney function and aortic aneurysms were included as control group. 27 were female, 84 cases were for thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm, while 106 cases were for abdominal aortic aneurysm. Primary endpoint was the freedom from contrast-induced acute kidney injury. Secondary safety endpoints were freedom from access site complications and cerebrovascular incidents. Imaging quality endpoints were attenuation values and contrast-to-noise-ratios in predefined vessels, validated by intraclass correlation coefficients.ResultsMean creatinine change was -.11 mg/dL, mean GFR change was 2.13% in the intervention group. There were 10 (4.6%) false aneurysms and two access site hematoma (0.93%). Two cerebrovascular incidents (0.9%) were transient. Transarterial CTA attenuation values varied between 210.4 (±89) and 241.4 (±98) Hounsfield units (HU), and 306.35 (±63.27) to 321.39 (±70.12) HU in the control group. The mean amount of contrast medium used in the catheter group was significantly reduced (31.70 ± 5.82 mL) compared to the control group (= .001). Contrast-to-noise ratios varied between 9.1 (±4.6) and 11.1 (±4.4. Intraclass correlation coefficients between the readings were very good (0.987-0.992).ConclusionCatheter-based transarterial computed tomographic angiography is a safe and efficacious way to evaluate patients with aortic aneurysms, both prior and after EVAR.

title: Perioperative management of acute type A aortic dissection using extended half-life factor IX (Alprolix) in a patient with severe hemophilia B: a case report.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Emergency surgery for acute type A aortic dissection (ATAAD) in patients with severe hemophilia B is extremely rare, and perioperative coagulation management is a major challenge. CASE PRESENTATION: A 63-year-old man with severe hemophilia B (factor IX activity < 1%) was diagnosed with ATAAD and underwent emergency surgery. Replacement therapy with an extended half-life factor IX product (eftrenonacog alfa; Alprolix) was administered targeting a factor IX activity of 80-100%, and total arch replacement was performed. Cardiopulmonary bypass was performed under standard heparinization conditions. Since rapid measurement of factor IX activity was not possible, postoperative replacement therapy was based primarily on the clinical assessment of hemostasis, with serial activated partial thromboplastin time measurements providing supportive information, whereas intraoperative anticoagulation was managed using standard activated clotting time monitoring. Intra- and postoperative bleeding volumes were within ranges comparable to those observed in standard complex aortic surgery, and the postoperative course was uneventful. CONCLUSIONS: The use of an extended half-life factor IX product may be a practical option for perioperative coagulation management during emergency aortic surgery in patients with severe hemophilia B.

title: Integrative genetic analyses for drug repurposing identify emodin as a candidate modulator of STAT3 signaling in abdominal aortic aneurysm.
abstract: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a life-threatening vascular disease lacking effective pharmacological therapies. To identify potential therapeutic targets and candidate compounds, we performed integrative genetic analyses for drug repurposing by combining Mendelian randomization (MR), summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR), and Bayesian colocalization. This framework prioritized multiple druggable candidates, among which STAT3 emerged as a key regulatory node. Subsequent functional studies demonstrated that emodin suppressed vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation, migration, phenotypic switching, and inflammatory responses. These effects were accompanied by reduced STAT3 phosphorylation and nuclear localization. Molecular docking suggested a potential binding mode of emodin within the STAT3 SH2 domain, while cellular thermal shift assays demonstrated thermal stabilization of STAT3 by emodin in intact cells, consistent with target engagement. Notably, emodin and the selective STAT3 inhibitor STAT3-IN-13 produced comparable effects, and co-treatment did not yield additive efficacy, suggesting overlapping mechanisms. In vivo, emodin attenuated aneurysm development and reduced vascular inflammation in experimental models. Collectively, these findings identify emodin as a candidate modulator of AAA progression acting through suppression of STAT3-associated signaling pathways, and demonstrate the potential of genetic evidence-guided drug repurposing strategies in complex vascular diseases.

title: Early and follow-up results of reinterventions for type 2 endoleak following endovascular repair of abdominal aortic aneurysm (EVAR): the multicenter REinterventions for Type 2 Endoleak (RETE) study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Type II endoleak (T2EL) is frequent after endovascular abdominal aortic aneurysm repair (EVAR) and may require reintervention in selected patients. However, the optimal treatment strategy for durable resolution remains uncertain. The aim of this study is to retrospectively analyze perioperative and long-term results of T2Els' reinterventions, both endovascular and open surgical, in a large patient cohort from twenty high-volume academic centers. METHODS: A retrospective analysis of consecutive patients undergoing first reintervention for T2ELs was conducted across 20 centers over a 10-year period. Patients requiring concomitant treatment for other endoleak types were excluded. A total of 403 patients were included. Primary outcomes included technical success, 30-day AAA-related mortality and reintervention-free survival during follow-up. Secondary outcomes were perioperative complications, early reintervention, overall survival, freedom from aneurysm-related death and rupture, freedom from recurrent endoleaks, freedom from open conversion or semi-conversion in patients previously treated endovascularly and sac behavior during follow-up. Kaplan-Meier curves and Cox regression analyses were performed to analyze follow-up results. RESULTS: Patients were predominantly male (90%) with a mean age of 77 years. Reintervention was indicated for sac enlargement in 94.5% of cases; 4% presented with rupture. Median time from EVAR to reintervention was 4.3 years. Lumbar arteries (55%) and the inferior mesenteric artery (35%) were the main sources. Endovascular treatment was performed in 86% and open conversion/semi-conversion in 14%. Technical success was 96%, with 1% mortality and 4% major complications. Overall survival was 80.5% and rupture-free survival 79.2% at 5 years. Recurrent T2EL occurred in 64.2%, and reintervention-free survival was 48.3%. Endovascular group showed significantly lower freedom from reintervention rates when compared to open conversion/semi conversion group (42.4% vs 86.8%, SE 0.04 vs SE 0.05, p<0.001, log-rank 15.9). Conversion/semi-conversion after endovascular treatment occurred in 14%. No differences were recorded comparing different fabric materials of the endograft in terms of freedom for reintervention and freedom from open surgery. A sac diameter ≥7 cm at the time of reintervention predicted further reinterventions, while primary open treatment improved durability. CONCLUSIONS: Reinterventions for T2ELs are safe, with satisfactory immediate technical success and low perioperative mortality. During follow-up, risks of rupture and AAA-related death remain low. However, the endoleak recurrence rate exceeds 60% at five years, necessitating reintervention in over 40% of patients. Early intervention for patients with a sac diameter approaching 7 cm can be suggested, while a primary open approach may be considered in low-risk patients.

However, the optimal treatment strategy for durable resolution remains uncertain. The aim of this study is to retrospectively analyze perioperative and long-term results of T2Els' reinterventions, both endovascular and open surgical, in a large patient cohort from twenty high-volume academic centers.

title: Risk Factors and Clinical Outcomes of Reocclusion after Endovascular Treatment for Acute Ischemic Stroke: An Updated Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Early reocclusion after endovascular treatment (EVT) for acute ischemic stroke is underrecognized; its determinants and impact remain poorly defined. METHODS: Random-effects meta-analysis of early reocclusion after successful EVT (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library through January 2026). Crude odds ratios (ORs) were pooled and certainty rated with GRADE. Post hoc sensitivity analyses included only same-site reocclusion definitions. RESULTS: Ten studies (3,381 patients) were included; 244 (7.2%) reoccluded. Reocclusion was associated with lower 90-day functional independence (OR 0.25, 95% CI 0.17-0.38) and higher mortality (OR 1.86, 1.29-2.68), both moderate certainty. Reocclusion was more frequent with large-artery atherosclerosis (OR 2.24, 1.41-3.55; same-site 3.04, 1.73-5.33) and less frequent with cardioembolism (OR 0.40, 0.28-0.57) and atrial fibrillation (OR 0.39, 0.26-0.59), mutually confounded associations reflecting one embolic-versus-atherothrombotic axis. Prestroke antiplatelet therapy (OR 0.43, 0.28-0.67) lost significance under the same-site definition (0.60, 0.31-1.16). Exploratory data (two cohorts) linked eTICI 2c-3 reperfusion with less reocclusion (OR 0.44, 0.28-0.69). No study reported when etiology was adjudicated; the atherosclerosis association may be partly outcome-induced. CONCLUSIONS: Early reocclusion is uncommon but carries a substantial prognostic penalty. Its determinants appear to lie in the vascular substrate rather than thrombectomy technique; prospective studies with uniform same-site definitions and systematic follow-up imaging are needed.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND: Early reocclusion after endovascular treatment (EVT) for acute ischemic stroke is underrecognized; its determinants and impact remain poorly defined. METHODS: Random-effects meta-analysis of early reocclusion after successful EVT (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library through January 2026). Crude odds ratios (ORs) were pooled and certainty rated with GRADE.

title: Does the HPB surgeon need a vascular surgeon?
abstract: Complex HPB surgery increasingly requires vascular resection and reconstruction. Therefore, vascular expertise is an essential part of surgical planning, technical execution, and oncological decision-making. While highly complex arterial, caval, or ex situ procedures should remain concentrated in specialised centres, every HPB surgeon should possess core vascular competence. Vascular and transplantation training should therefore become an integral part of advanced HPB education.

title: Effect of Extended-Duration Venous Thromboprophylaxis After Cancer Surgery.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cancer patients undergoing surgery are at significantly increased risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE). Although extended thromboprophylaxis is recommended, the optimal anticoagulant type and duration remain unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the comparative efficacy and safety of different extended thromboprophylaxis in this population. METHODS: A Bayesian network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was performed to evaluate various thromboprophylaxis strategies for patients undergoing cancer-related surgery. We conducted both three-node and five-node network analyses to evaluate extended-duration versus standard-duration thromboprophylaxis strategies. Outcomes included venous thromboembolism, major bleeding, and all-cause mortality. Net clinical benefit and risk-benefit assessments were additionally performed to determine the overall impact of prolonged anticoagulant therapy. Treatment effects were summarized as risk ratios (RRs) with corresponding 95% credible intervals (CrIs). RESULTS: A total of 14 randomized controlled trials involving 4,331 participants were included. Compared with placebo, extended-duration prophylaxis with direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) (RR 0.12, 95% CrI 0.05-0.27) and low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) (RR 0.17, 95% CrI 0.05-0.55) significantly reduced the incidence of venous thromboembolism without a corresponding increase in major bleeding. In net clinical benefit analyses, both prolonged DOAC therapy (RR 0.27, 95% CrI 0.14-0.49) and LMWH (RR 0.36, 95% CrI 0.17-0.76) demonstrated favorable overall outcomes. Risk-benefit evaluation suggested that prolonged DOACs provided a more advantageous balance than LMWH, with an NNH/NNT ratio of 4.17. CONCLUSIONS: Extended thromboprophylaxis is effective and safe for cancer patients undergoing surgery. Besides, DOACs appears to be the optimal anticoagulant for extended thromboprophylaxis, providing the greatest net clinical benefit.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND: Cancer patients undergoing surgery are at significantly increased risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE). Although extended thromboprophylaxis is recommended, the optimal anticoagulant type and duration remain unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the comparative efficacy and safety of different extended thromboprophylaxis in this population.

title: Computer tomography imaging for suspected acute aortic syndrome.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Acute Aortic Syndrome (AAS) is a life-threatening condition that presents diagnostic challenges due to variable clinical presentations. Limited data exists regarding Computed Tomography Angiography (CTA) utilisation patterns and outcomes for patients with suspected AAS in Irish emergency departments (ED). This study evaluates trends in CTA utilisation and positivity rate for patients with suspected AAS presenting to a level 4 hospital ED. METHODS: A retrospective single-centre chart review was conducted of all adult patients (≥ 16 years) who underwent CTA aorta imaging requested by emergency medicine physicians in Tallaght University Hospital between January 2018 and December 2025. Patient demographics, imaging findings, time metrics, disposition and mortality were analysed. RESULTS: Among 457,735 ED attendances, 797 eligible CTA aorta studies were performed. There was a 2.86 fold increase in CTA scans done across the study period from 37 studies in 2018 to 106 in 2025. Overall positivity rate for AAS was 2.76% (n = 22). Acute aortic dissection accounted for 77% of positive cases (n = 17), followed by penetrating atherosclerotic ulcers (n = 3) and intramural hematomas (n = 2). Overall mortality among patients with confirmed AAS was 27.27%. CONCLUSION: This study highlights the low positivity rate of CTA aorta scans in an Irish ED but high mortality of patients diagnosed with acute aortic syndrome. Increasing CTA utilisation, alongside the overall low incidence of AAS, suggests opportunities to improve diagnostic efficiency.

Limited data exists regarding Computed Tomography Angiography (CTA) utilisation patterns and outcomes for patients with suspected AAS in Irish emergency departments (ED). This study evaluates trends in CTA utilisation and positivity rate for patients with suspected AAS presenting to a level 4 hospital ED.

title: An enlarged nonfistulous artery mimicking an additional feeder in a pediatric pial arteriovenous fistula: an angiographic pitfall.
abstract: Pial arteriovenous fistulas (PAVFs) are rare high-flow vascular lesions requiring precise characterization of the fistulous angioarchitecture before treatment. We report a pediatric PAVF in which an enlarged artery adjacent to the fistula initially appeared suspicious for additional fistulous supply. Superselective angiography demonstrated normal cortical arterial arborization and parenchymal perfusion without early venous drainage, confirming that the enlarged vessel did not participate directly in the arteriovenous shunt. Selective coil embolization achieved complete immediate occlusion of the fistulous communication while preserving the adjacent normal cortical arterial supply. This case illustrates that arterial enlargement alone does not establish participation in a PAVF and highlights an angiographic pitfall relevant to treatment planning.

title: Characterizing the Thrombotic Spectrum and Clinical Phenotypes of Tranexamic Acid-Associated Adverse Events: A Pharmacovigilance Study Based on the FAERS Database.
abstract: Tranexamic acid (TXA) is widely used to reduce bleeding in surgical, trauma, obstetric, and gynecological settings. However, concerns remain regarding TXA-associated thrombotic adverse events, and their phenotypic heterogeneity and clinical severity have not been comprehensively characterized. This study investigated TXA-associated thrombotic events using the Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) from 2004Q1 to 2026Q1. Thrombotic adverse events were identified using the Standardized MedDRA Query (SMQ) "Embolic and thrombotic events" and evaluated by disproportionality analysis based on reporting odds ratios (RORs). Qualifying thrombotic events were assigned to the SMQ vessel-type subgroups-arterial, vessel-type unspecified/mixed, and venous-and demographic characteristics, indications, clinical outcomes and time-to-onset were compared across subgroups; signal strength was further related to clinical severity. In all, 515 thrombotic cases associated with TXA and 26 selected thrombotic terms were found (arterial, 157; mixed, 168; venous, 190). Venous thromboembolism-pulmonary embolism (n = 128, ROR 13.94) and deep vein thrombosis (n = 58, ROR 9.09)-is the most frequent type and brings about the most severe and fatal consequences (death reported in 16.8% of venous versus 2.5% of arterial reports), whereas the strongest disproportionality signals were observed for rare site-specific events such as ovarian vein thrombosis (ROR 352.95) and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (ROR 118.35). The three subgroups differed markedly in demographic and clinical characteristics: venous events occurred predominantly in women (73.7%) treated for menorrhagia (35.3%), whereas arterial events arose mainly in surgical or procedural settings (intravenous route 36.3%; surgery/prophylaxis 19.1%) and presented earliest after exposure [median time-to-onset (TTO) 0 versus 7 days]. Signal strength was not concordant with clinical severity across the thrombotic spectrum. These findings provide a deeper understanding of the thrombotic safety of TXA, indicate that the clinical background may influence the phenotypic differences among the different thrombotic types, and emphasize the necessity of enhanced attention and risk stratification in high-risk groups.

However, concerns remain regarding TXA-associated thrombotic adverse events, and their phenotypic heterogeneity and clinical severity have not been comprehensively characterized. This study investigated TXA-associated thrombotic events using the Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) from 2004Q1 to 2026Q1.

title: Association between thyroid feedback quantile-based index and the risk of in-hospital amputation in patients with diabetic foot ulcer.
abstract: AIMS: To investigate the relationship between the thyroid feedback quantile-based index (TFQI) and the risk of amputation during hospitalization in patients with diabetic foot ulcers (DFU). METHODS: This single-center retrospective study included 381 hospitalized patients with DFU and normal thyroid function. Logistic regression assessed continuous TFQI and quartiles. Model 1 was unadjusted; Model 2 adjusted for age, sex, BMI, and smoking; Model 3 additionally adjusted for diabetes duration, HbA1c, diabetic peripheral neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease, hypertension, CRP, and dyslipidemia. RCS assessed dose-response patterns; Firth regression was used for sensitivity analysis. RESULTS: Fifty-six patients underwent amputation. In Model 3, each 1-SD increase in TFQI (equivalent to a 1-unit increase in pre-scaled TFQI) was associated with higher odds of amputation (OR 2.27, 95% CI 1.63-3.15; P < 0.001). Compared with Q1, ORs were 2.94 (0.98-8.83; P = 0.055), 5.60 (1.88-16.67; P = 0.002), and 14.79 (5.22-41.89; P < 0.001) for Q2, Q3, and Q4, respectively. RCS showed an overall association (P = 0.002) and nonlinearity (P = 0.046) in Model 3. Firth estimates were broadly consistent with conventional regression. CONCLUSION: Among hospitalized DFU patients with normal thyroid function, higher TFQI levels are associated with an increased risk of amputation during hospitalization. Nevertheless, the clinical utility of TFQI requires further validation in prospective studies.

METHODS: This single-center retrospective study included 381 hospitalized patients with DFU and normal thyroid function. Logistic regression assessed continuous TFQI and quartiles.

title: Percutaneous and Endovascular Embolization-Based Treatments of Type 1A and Type 1B Endoleaks after Endovascular Aneurysm Repair.
abstract: ObjectiveThis retrospective, observational study was conducted to evaluate the efficacy of embolization-based treatments for Types 1A and 1B endoleaks following endovascular aneurysm repair.DesignA total of 26 patients who underwent endovascular aneurysm repair between January 2005 and September 2023 and subsequently received embolization therapy for Types 1A or 1B endoleak, either at the end of the procedure or during follow-up, were retrospectively reviewed.MethodsEmbolization was performed in 16 patients with Type 1A endoleaks and 10 with Type 1B. Eight of the 16 patients who underwent embolization for Type 1A endoleaks required additional treatments such as aortic cuff placement or a chimney graft. Similarly, six out of the 10 patients treated with embolization for Type 1B endoleaks underwent adjunctive procedures such as iliac stent-graft extension. The primary endpoint was the absence of aneurysm sac enlargement. Secondary endpoints included technical success and the avoidance of endoleak-related reintervention.ResultsAneurysm sac regression or stabilization was observed in 68.7% of Type 1A and 70% of Type 1B endoleak cases over mean follow-up periods of 43.1 and 22.3 months, respectively.ConclusionEmbolization-based endovascular treatment, alone or combined with adjunctive endograft procedures, may achieve aneurysm sac stabilization or regression in a substantial proportion of patients with Types 1A and 1B endoleaks. However, the possibility of recurrence and reintervention, particularly in Type 1A endoleaks, remains an important limitation of this approach and warrants continued imaging surveillance.

title: EXPRESS: Cerebral blood flow-oxygen metabolism uncoupling at 24 hours after stroke thrombectomy.
abstract: BackgroundFollowing successful endovascular therapy (EVT) for acute ischemic stroke, tissue with abnormal perfusion may have impaired oxygen extraction and metabolism. MRI model-based oxygen extraction fraction (OEFmax) and cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO2) were characterized in hypoperfusion and hyperemia regions 24 hours post-EVT.MethodsEighty-four patients were included with anterior circulation vessel occlusion, successful recanalization, and an MRI at 24 hours post-EVT. Time-to-maximum (Tmax) and cerebral blood flow (CBF) were evaluated for hypoperfusion and hyperemia. CBF, OEFmax, and CMRO2 were quantified using i) segmentation-based and ii) single slice region of interest (ROI) analyses. Normalized CBF, OEFmax, and CMRO2 were calculated by dividing the segmentation or ROI value by the contralateral value.ResultsSixty-seven (80%) patients had abnormal perfusion; hypoperfusion in 22 (26%), hyperemia in 36 (43%), and both in 9 (11%). Compared to control, hypoperfused regions demonstrated a 62% CBF decrease, 52% CMRO2 decrease, and 68% OEFmax increase (p<0.01). Hyperemic regions demonstrated a 58% CBF increase, 26% CMRO2 increase, and 25% OEFmax decrease (p<0.01). Hyperemia had no significant correlation between normalized CBF and CMRO2 (p=0.14).ConclusionHyperemia regions demonstrated cerebral blood flow-oxygen metabolism uncoupling, suggesting the underlying mechanism as loss of cerebrovascular autoregulation rather than hypermetabolic demand.

Time-to-maximum (Tmax) and cerebral blood flow (CBF) were evaluated for hypoperfusion and hyperemia.

title: Venous sinus of Kelch: a cadaveric study with embryological insights and clinical implications.
abstract: The venous sinus of Kelch (VSK) represents a rare but clinically significant venous variant of the middle cranial fossa, with very limited documentation in the existing literature. This study aimed to understand the morphology, course, and morphometry of VSK along with associated variations in the drainage pattern of the superficial middle cerebral vein (SMCV) and middle meningeal sinus (MMS). This study was conducted over the period from 2022 to 2025 at Zoram Medical College and Hospital, Aizawl, Mizoram. In the present study, VSK was observed in 9.26% of the 54 middle cranial fossae examined from 27 cadavers. Moreover, SMCV and MMS, which normally drain into either the spheno-parietal sinus or cavernous sinus, drained into VSK. From an embryological perspective, VSK can be understood as a persistent primitive tentorial sinus (PTS). The variable course and termination of PTS may also result in other reported venous variants like Spheno-basal sinus, Spheno-petrosal sinus and Petro-basal sinus, which underscore the complexity of venous adaptations influenced by hemodynamic factors. Clinically, awareness of such variants is crucial for accurate radiological interpretation and for minimising the risk of iatrogenic injury during surgical and endovascular procedures involving the middle cranial fossa. Importantly, recognition of these alternative venous pathways may have future implications in facilitating novel endovascular approaches for neuromodulation, targeted therapy, and minimally invasive access to the temporal lobe and trigeminal nerve.

title: Use of vaginal estrogens in urogynecology: current evidence, controversies and clinical applications.
abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM) is a prevalent yet underrecognized condition in postmenopausal women, characterized by progressive vulvovaginal and lower urinary tract symptoms from estrogen deficiency. Vaginal estrogen therapy is the first-line pharmacologic treatment for GSM. However, as new evidence emerges, understanding of its efficacy, safety, and use in special populations continues to evolve. This review summarizes current evidence on vaginal estrogen formulations, clinical effectiveness, safety, and therapeutic applications. RECENT FINDINGS: Recent randomized controlled trials confirm that low-dose vaginal estrogen significantly improves GSM symptoms - including vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, and irritation - while restoring epithelial integrity and normalizing pH. Evidence also supports its role in reducing recurrent urinary tract infections by restoring lactobacilli-dominant flora, reinforced by a 2025 multisociety clinical guideline recommending topical, but not systemic, estrogen for this indication. Comparative studies show similar efficacy across creams, tablets, inserts, and rings, differing primarily in convenience and absorption rather than effectiveness. Large cohort studies indicate no increased risk of cardiovascular disease, venous thromboembolism, or malignancy. Use in breast cancer survivors remains controversial, but emerging data suggest minimal systemic absorption and no clear increase in recurrence risk, supporting shared decision-making. In addition, long-term outcomes show that adjunctive vaginal estrogen does not improve anatomic surgical success after native tissue apical prolapse repair. Nonhormonal therapies and agents like ospemifene or prasterone offer alternative options, though they demonstrate lower or more variable efficacy than vaginal estrogen. SUMMARY: Vaginal estrogen therapy is the most effective, evidence-based treatment for GSM and helps prevent recurrent urinary tract infections in postmenopausal women. Its favorable safety profile and multiple formulations enable individualized care. Recent evidence clarifies that while overall safety is reassuring, caution is necessary for breast cancer survivors using aromatase inhibitors. Additionally, longer-term perioperative trial data temper expectations regarding surgical-recurrence benefits, while confirming its value for local tissue optimization. Ongoing research should focus on long-term safety in high-risk groups and the effectiveness of emerging non-estrogen alternatives.

Vaginal estrogen therapy is the first-line pharmacologic treatment for GSM. However, as new evidence emerges, understanding of its efficacy, safety, and use in special populations continues to evolve.

title: Ultrasound-Guided versus Fluoroscopy-Guided Femoral Access for Structural Heart Procedures: Outcomes From Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation and Left Atrial Appendage Closure.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Transfemoral access is the default approach for transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) and left atrial appendage closure (LAAC). Although ultrasound (US)-guided femoral puncture improves first-pass success and reduces vascular complications in randomized trials, real-world data in contemporary structural heart interventions, including both arterial and venous large-sheath access, remain limited. The authors aimed to compare US-guided vs. conventional transfemoral access in patients undergoing TAVI and LAAC. METHODS: This single-center, retrospective cohort study included 165 consecutive patients undergoing transfemoral structural procedures between January 2022 and December 2024 (93: TAVI; 72: LAAC). Ultrasound guidance was used in 57 procedures (34.5%). Arterial and venous cohorts were analyzed separately. Primary outcomes were absolute hemoglobin decrease (ΔHb) and access-site vascular complications (hematoma, pseudoaneurysm, and arteriovenous fistula). In the arterial cohort, 1 : 1 propensity score matching was performed to adjust for baseline differences. RESULTS: Hemoglobin decline was significantly smaller with US guidance in both venous (0.80 ± 0.95 vs. 1.50 ± 1.11 g/dL; P = .009) and arterial procedures (0.58 ± 0.97 vs. 1.29 ± 1.00 g/dL; P = .002). In the venous cohort, complication rates were numerically lower but not statistically different (3.8% vs. 17.4%; P = .143). In contrast, arterial complications were significantly reduced with US guidance. After propensity matching (31 patients per group), complications occurred in 3.2% vs. 29.0% [Absolute Risk Reduction(ARR) = 25.8%, Number Need to Treat (NNT) = 4, P = .013]. CONCLUSIONS: Ultrasound-guided transfemoral access was associated with reduced hemoglobin decline and fewer vascular complications, particularly in large-bore arterial procedures, supporting routine integration of real-time US guidance in structural interventions.

title: Hemodynamic and Geometrical Parameters Associated with Carotid Artery Stenosis: A Cross-Sectional Study Using 4D Flow MRI and CFD.
abstract: PURPOSE: Carotid geometry and local hemodynamics are closely associated with atherosclerosis, yet how anatomy and disturbed flow jointly mark disease presence and relate to pro-atherogenic flow in still-non-stenosed bifurcations remains unresolved. This study quantifies the cross-sectional association between three-dimensional carotid bifurcation geometry and pro-atherogenic flow and identifies anatomical biomarkers for non-invasive risk stratification. METHODS: Geometric analyses included 346 carotid bifurcations, comprising 240 stenosed and 106 non-stenosed bifurcations. Patient-specific CFD was performed in 176 bifurcations: 101 stenosed and 75 non-stenosed. Eight geometric descriptors, including a new offset flow divider capturing bifurcation apex asymmetry, and four ICA bulb hemodynamic indices (TAWSS, OSI, RRT, BFI) were extracted; logistic and linear regression assessed the association of geometry with (i) stenosis presence and (ii) pro-atherogenic flow. RESULTS: p < 0.001 AUROC = 0.767 60 % Bifurcation angle, ICA angle, tortuosity, and offset flow divider were significantly elevated in stenosed bifurcations (all); a four-feature geometric model showed moderate discrimination between stenosed and non-stenosed bifurcations (cross-validated). The post-stenotic expansion ratio was more strongly associated with local flow disturbance than the degree of luminal narrowing. In non-stenosed bifurcations, multivariable geometric models explained 49 toof the variance in the flow-normalized low-TAWSS, elevated-OSI, and elevated-RRT outcomes, with bulb area and area ratio providing the largest independent contributions, indicating that geometric variation is strongly associated with candidate pro-atherogenic flow patterns even in the absence of detectable luminal narrowing. CONCLUSIONS: Carotid geometry carries two complementary signals: markers of disease presence (bifurcation angle, ICA angle) and candidate anatomical substrates of pro-atherogenic flow in still-non-stenosed bifurcations (bulb area, area ratio). Together with the post-stenotic expansion ratio, these geometric features define a compact, image-derivable set of candidate biomarkers for future early carotid risk stratification.

title: Access Vessel Patency After Endovascular Therapy via Tibiopedal Access in Patients With Lower Extremity Artery Disease.
abstract: PURPOSE: This study aimed to evaluate the access vessel patency after endovascular therapy performed via tibiopedal access. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This was a retrospective, single-center, observational study. Patients who underwent endovascular therapy via tibiopedal access with sheath insertion were enrolled. The primary outcome was loss of access vessel patency defined as access vessel occlusion or stenosis with a peak systolic velocity ratio > 2.4 on duplex ultrasound at 6 months. Multivariate logistic regression analysis was performed to identify the predictors of access vessel patency loss, with hemodialysis, severely calcified access vessel and sheath-to-artery ratio included as covariates. RESULTS: A total of 95 limbs in 91 patients were included in this study, and loss of access vessel patency was observed in 22 limbs (23.1%). Multivariate logistic regression analysis demonstrated that sheath-to-artery ratio was the only independent predictor (odds ratio: 1.493, 95% confidence interval: 1.130-1.976; p = 0.005). The receiver operating characteristic curve analysis revealed that the optimal cutoff value of sheath-to-artery ratio for predicting loss of access vessel patency was 1.08, with an area under the curve of 0.723. In this cohort, the 2-year freedom from major adverse limb events were 98.6% (95% CI: 90.8-99.8%), and no major amputation occurred. CONCLUSION: The present study demonstrated a relatively high incidence of loss of access vessel patency after endovascular therapy via tibiopedal access, although this was not associated with an increase in major adverse limb events. A larger sheath-to-artery ratio was identified as an independent predictor of loss of access vessel patency.

title: Sex differences in lipid-lowering therapy after atherothrombotic ischemic stroke: The multicenter MaLIC study.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Women have poorer outcomes after ischaemic stroke. The primary objective was to assess sex-based differences in the management and intensity of lipid-lowering therapy following non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA). Secondary objectives were to analyse sex-based differences in vascular risk profile, pre-event functional status, and stroke severity. MATERIAL AND METHODS: Subanalysis of the second phase of the MaLIC study (Management of Stroke in Catalonia and the Balearic Islands), a prospective, multicentre study conducted in 20 hospitals. Adults with non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke or TIA were included. Vascular risk factors, stroke severity, lipid profile, and intensity of lipid-lowering therapy at hospital discharge were compared according to sex. RESULTS: A total of 591 patients were included, of whom 223 (37.7%) were women. Women were older (76 vs. 70 years; P<.0001), had greater pre-event functional dependence (mRS>2: 16.1% vs. 7.9%; P=.003), and a lower prevalence of ischaemic heart disease (4.9% vs. 14.4%; P<0001) and peripheral arterial disease (6.3% vs. 13.0%; P=.01). Although women had higher LDL cholesterol levels at admission (103.5 vs. 92mg/dl; P=.004), they were less frequently prescribed high-intensity lipid-lowering therapy at discharge (64.1% vs. 72.3%; P=.04). No differences were observed in stroke code activation or reperfusion therapies. CONCLUSIONS: Women were less frequently prescribed high-intensity lipid-lowering therapy at discharge than men, despite having higher LDL cholesterol levels. These findings highlight an opportunity to optimise lipid-lowering therapy after the cerebrovascular event.

The primary objective was to assess sex-based differences in the management and intensity of lipid-lowering therapy following non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA). Secondary objectives were to analyse sex-based differences in vascular risk profile, pre-event functional status, and stroke severity.

title: A Study on Renal Artery Variations by CT Angiography and Their Clinical Importance.
abstract: AimThis study aimed to evaluate the prevalence, anatomical variations, and branching patterns of the renal arteries using multiphasic computed tomography angiography (CTA), based on the modified classification proposed by Cases et al (2017). Understanding renal artery variations is essential for preoperative planning, renal transplantation, endovascular procedures, and urological interventions.Materials and MethodsA retrospective analysis was conducted on 1220 abdominal CTA studies performed between March 2020 and June 2024. Fourteen cases were excluded according to predetermined exclusion criteria, resulting in 1206 studies being included in the final analysis (700 males, 520 females). All examinations were performed using a 128-slice CT scanner (Siemens SOMATOM; syngo CT VC 40). CTA protocols included 5-mm acquisition and 1-mm reconstruction, with administration of 100-120 mL of iodinated contrast at 5-6 mL/s via an 18G antecubital cannula. Post-processing involved multiplanar reformation, volume rendering, and 3D reconstruction. Two experienced radiologists independently reviewed all studies. Renal arteries were categorized into Types A-E and Patterns I-V. "Early division" (Types B and E) and "polar branches" (Types C and D) were further grouped for analytical purposes.ResultsAmong 1206 CTA studies, Type A (normal hilar artery) was the most common in both kidneys, with a slightly higher prevalence on the right (74.29%) than on the left (67.99%). Polar branches were more frequent in the left kidney, whereas early divisions were more common in the right kidney. Pattern 1 was predominant bilaterally (RK: 85.73%; LK: 77.61%), followed by Pattern 2. Significant differences were observed between the kidneys in the distribution of Types A, C, D, and Patterns 1 and 2.ConclusionCTA provides excellent visualization of renal artery variations, enabling precise classification and improving surgical, interventional, and transplant planning. Recognition of these anatomical differences is essential for minimizing procedural complications.

title: Endovascular Salvage of Dysfunctional Native Haemodialysis Arteriovenous Fistulas: Clinical Outcomes and Predictors of Patency.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Hypofunctioning haemodialysis arteriovenous fistulas are an important cause of inadequate dialysis, access failure and morbidity in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), and timely catheter-based intervention may help restore access function and prolong fistula usability. OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the efficacy, feasibility, and safety of catheter-based interventional procedures for hypofunctioning haemodialysis fistulas in patients with CKD. METHODS: This single-centre, retrospective observational follow up study, enrolled with 100 CKD patients on maintenance haemodialysis with dysfunctional native arteriovenous fistulas who underwent fistulogram and catheter-based intervention. RESULTS: The mean age was 57.2 ± 12.4 years, 62.0% were male, and hypertension (80.0%) and diabetes mellitus (57.0%) were the major comorbidities. Radio cephalic fistula was the commonest access type (46.0%), and inadequate dialysis was the leading presentation (73.0%). Fistulography showed significant stenosis in 96.0%, with central vein involvement in 43.0% and long-segment lesions in 56.0%. Angioplasty was attempted in 96.0%, achieving technical success in 91.7% of attempted interventions and clinical success in 85.0%. Stenosis and pressure gradient reduced significantly after intervention (both p<0.001). Complications occurred in 13.0%, with no deaths. Primary patency declined from 82.0% at 1 month to 58.0% at 6 months and 38.0% at 12 months. Patency loss was independently predicted by older age, central vein lesions, long lesions, residual stenosis, and absent post-procedure thrill. CONCLUSION: Catheter-based endovascular intervention may be an effective fistula-salvage strategy for hypofunctioning haemodialysis arteriovenous fistulas, although long-term patency was influenced by lesion complexity, residual stenosis and restoration of post-procedure thrill.

METHODS: This single-centre, retrospective observational follow up study, enrolled with 100 CKD patients on maintenance haemodialysis with dysfunctional native arteriovenous fistulas who underwent fistulogram and catheter-based intervention.
